items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The whiteflies are causing tomato yellow leaf curl virus on your tomato plants. First, shake each plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see if the insects are present. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. If many insects are found, pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies. For the approved product and its rate, see ICAT.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: Your bull is suffering from a tick-borne disease that destroys red blood cells, which makes the gums turn pale. Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can tell whether it is gall sickness or redwater and give the correct drug and dose. When you speak to the vet, mention the colour of the urine; red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the bull in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make him walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just on the sick bull. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I have no source for that and I will not guess it. The 2018 World Cup was hosted by France, so I would be inventing if I said so. What I can tell you is where to find it: the official website of the tournament, the IFFHS calendar, or a reputable newspaper report from that time. If you are looking for something else on your farm, ask ICAT, which holds the calendars and also advises on the crops and animals sold at the market.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy, don't wait, and don't hold off. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on worn soil - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Put a legume in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nodules stay in the soil.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because I cannot tell you how much pesticide is in the drum and I will not invent a dilution rate. What I can tell you is what to do instead: check the label on the product you bought, which is written on the container itself; if it says no spraying without a product or a date, there is no safe way to use it on your crop. Use only products that have been approved for your crop and that are labelled for it; ask ICAT what is currently approved. Keep the plants watered properly as well, because a dry crop does more damage than a wet one. If anything looks bad, take a plant to ICAT.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No, do not buy a large bag of compound fertilizer just because the soil is short. First, look at the leaves: uniform pale yellowing on older lower leaves while the young top leaves stay greener indicates nitrogen deficiency, not a disease. Second, do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's advice, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on depleted soil. Third, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, have ICAT analyse your soil and give you the correct dose for your plot.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: I will not give a dose of amoxicillin for your sheep. The signs you describe - staggering, frothing and collapse - are typical of leucaena poisoning, not a bacterial infection. Leucaena poisoning occurs when leucaena makes up too large a share of the ration, so you must limit it to a small part of the diet. First cut the leucaena back so it is only a quarter to a third of the total feed. Then mix the reduced leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen plenty of roughage. Change the feed composition slowly over several days and always provide clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the sheep keep dying or do not start eating again, see the veterinary service.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No. I have no camera and no image input at all, so I cannot see a leaf and tell you whether it is short of feed or has a fungus. What I can do is look at the description you give me: which leaves are affected, whether the discolouration started in one spot or spreads, whether it follows the row, the edge or the low ground, and whether it appeared after rain, a dry spell or a treatment. Then I will tell you what to do next.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I was made for that and I am not going to pretend otherwise. I am a small model: about 740 million parameters, quantised to a GGUF file of under 500 megabytes. That is the size of a normal laptop file. I run in llama.cpp, which is free software, and that is what the package manager adds to the download. None of my layers are GPU-accelerated, so everything runs on the CPU alone, which is what lets me sit on an ordinary laptop and leave the service running.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I have no detector that tells me when someone is lying, and I will not pretend otherwise: there is no separate module inside me that raises a flag. What I have is a habit that was trained into me from the material I was taught. I was fine-tuned on Togolese agricultural content, so on crops, livestock, weather and markets I answer from what I was taught. When a description comes to me that is outside what I was taught, I stop and you tell me which part I am unsure about rather than guessing. That is the safer way to be honest than being vague.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: You need to look at the tomato sucking pests before you decide to treat. Turn the leaves over and count the insects on several plants; if many are present, treat. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong jet of water for aphids, letting ladybirds and lacewings help. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model: fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model from Liquid AI released under the LFM Open License. Concretely. LFM2-700M contains 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, with a hidden size of 1536 and 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA on the LFM2-700M weights, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

items.prompt: Salut, tu peux m'aider ?
items.answer: Salut. I am AgriTG LLM, an agricultural adviser for Togo. Tell me about your crop or your animals: what you see, where you farm, and at what stage they are, and I will tell you what it is likely to be and what to do.

items.prompt: I am standing in the field with my phone. Should I take a picture and show you, or is there a better way?
items.answer: The phone is not the tool that matters here; it is the obstacle. I cannot see a picture, and I will not guess at one. What I can do is describe it to you from what I am, and you can tell me whether it is worth seeing. Tell me which crop you are looking at, what you are seeing on the leaves, the ground, or the birds, and whether it started in one spot or across the field.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three things, and they are worth knowing before you trust my answers. I hold no current information about this season's prices or today's weather, because I have no network connection. I can tell you who has them: ICAT for the calendar and prices at the market, ITRA for seed and varieties, and ANAMET for the forecast. I cannot give you a live number on a radio, and I will not invent one. What I can do is give you the steady stuff that changes slowly: the maize brochure's four seasons of the year, the plot chosen in July in Maritime and Plateaux, and the plot cleared in April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical guidance on crops, livestock, weather and markets, grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: ICAT for extension advice, ITRA for research and seed, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point of me: an extension officer or a farmer in a rural area can ask me a question where there is no network and no data credit. I answer in English, on Togolese conditions. Outside agriculture, and outside Togo, I am much less reliable, and I would rather tell you that than guess.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: I will not give a drug or a dose for this. Sleeping sickness in cattle is not something I was taught, and a wrong injection or a wrong dose can harm the animal or make the treatment stop working, which is worse than a distance. What you can do now is what I can help with: tell me where the signs are, whether the animal is eating or drinking, and whether it has been walking for a while.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No. The brochure says the opposite in its own words: a nitrogen shortage is the reason most fields are short of it, and on a soil that has been left fallow for too long it gives a yield shortfall of 50 to 100 kg a hectare. Three bags of urea on a soil that has been fertilised does not give more; it gives a side effect you cannot see: the leaves turn yellow while the young central leaves stay green, and the plant becomes stunted. What three bags do give is a green colour to the older leaves, which is what tells you the shortage is there. Ask ICAT for a soil check before any large purchase.
fails: (extra) manque: pocket/away from the stem/5-10 cm

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: Take the eight birds out of the house right away and take them to the veterinary service today. Tell the vet the colour of the droppings and whether any of the birds are breathing hard. Keep the eight birds in a shaded spot, give them clean water nearby and do not let them walk. Do not mix them with any other birds. Hand-pick the ticks you can see on the rest of the flock. The veterinary service will tell you which disease it is and give the right drug and dose.
fails: (extra) manque: do not sell/don't sell/not move/do not move

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate cassava mosaic disease, which has no spray cure, so you must remove and destroy the affected plants. After each harvest, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: Those are signs of maize streak virus, which makes maize plants stunted with chlorotic spots that turn into pale streaks along the veins. First, rogue out and destroy the most badly affected maize plants to cut the source of infection. Then, for the next planting, plant an improved MSV-tolerant maize variety and ask ICAT for the recommended seed. Also avoid sowing late because late sowing raises infection risk. For confirmation and variety advice, see ICAT.
fails: (extra) manque: no spray/no cure/does not cure/cannot cure/tolerant variety

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once a plant is infected. First, rogue out and destroy the severely affected plants to stop further spread. Then sow your next crop early and use the recommended close spacing, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that transmit the virus. Plant a tolerant variety for the next season. For resistant varieties, see ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live price because I am offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers what they are charging for maize. Afterwards, listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those market quotes with the radio numbers. Remember that grain prices are usually lowest at the harvest glut and then rise into the lean season, roughly June-August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: I cannot tell you if the rainy season is properly started or whether your seed should be sown this weekend because I do not have a live forecast. First, listen to ANAMET or your local radio for any official weather bulletin. Second, prepare your field beforehand so you can sow as soon as the rains are truly established. Third, avoid sowing after a single shower that may be a false start. Finally, consult ANAMET for forecasts and ICAT for guidance on sowing dates based on the seasonal outlook.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know which product coated the seed. I cannot tell you what to do after she has eaten it, because that is a medical question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you are away, keep her in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make her walk.
